newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech government support wanes as economy sours.
newsitem.headline: Czech government support wanes as economy sours.

text.p: Public support for the Czech Republic's ruling centre-right coalition fell after a sharp drop in the crown and the launch of an emergency economic plan, an opinion poll released on Wednesday showed.
The survey, taken by the state Institute for Public Opinion Research (IVVM) from May 30 to June 3, showed combined support for the three-party coalition dropping to its lowest level yet,
But the popularity of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's right-wing Civic Democratic Party (ODS) edged slightly higher.
The percentage of potential voters saying they would vote for the ODS rose two percentage points, from its worst showing ever in an early-May IVVM poll, to 20 percent.
But falling support for the two junior coalition parties pushed overall support for the government down to 38.5 percent from 42.5.

The survey was conducted several days before the government narrowly won a parliamentary vote of confidence on Tuesday as the backing of one independent deputy gave the cabinet the decisive 101st vote in the 200-seat chamber.
The poll was carried out soon after the coalition announced an emergency austerity programme on May 28 and acknowledged earlier policy mistakes.
The plan included extensive budget cuts and public sector wage freezes aimed at slowing demand and bolstering the crown.
The currency has lost roughly 15 percent of its value since February, when it came under speculative attack which forced the central bank to float it.

The junior coalition parties, the pro-business Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) and the centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) saw their support in the poll fall to seven and 11.5 percent resepctively from 10 and 14.5 percent a month ago.
The largest opposition party, the centre-left Social Democrats, led all parties in the survey, rising to 28 percent from 25 percent, the highest level ever in IVVM polls.
The combined popularity of the opposition parties, including the far-left Communists and ultra-right Republicans, rose to 40 percent from 34 percent.

The Social Democrats have made soundings about forming a possible coalition with the Christian Democrats should the current government fall, but they have ruled out any coalition with the Republicans and the Communists.
The next general elections are scheduled for June 2000, but Social Democrat leaders have said that they expect early elections to be needed by the autumn of next year.
